1.tip: 12 bits = 4096 values = enough for every VLAN. Extended system ID holds the VLAN ID.
1.why: The bridge ID splits its priority field so 12 bits carry the VLAN ID. That lets a switch run a separate spanning tree per VLAN, each with its own bridge ID.

2.cue: first step of the spanning-tree election

keys.k: advertising themselves as the root bridge

2.tip: At boot, every switch thinks: I am the root! Then they compare BPDUs and the lowest bridge ID wins.
2.why: When switches start, none knows who is best, so each one claims to be the root in its BPDUs. They then compare bridge IDs and stop claiming once they hear a lower one.

3.cue: no other port with a lower cost to the root bridge
3.tip: Root port = my best (cheapest) road to the root. One per non-root switch.
3.why: Each non-root switch picks the one port with the lowest total cost to reach the root bridge. That port becomes its root port.

4.cue: only end devices attached, never another switch
4.tip: Edge of the network = edge port. Cisco's name for it = PortFast. Both skip the slow STP wait.
4.why: A port that only connects PCs or printers can't create a loop, so it can jump straight to forwarding. RSTP calls it an edge port and Cisco turns it on with PortFast.

5.cue: combined to form a bridge ID
5.tip: Bridge ID = P + E + M: Priority, Extended system ID (VLAN), MAC.
5.why: The bridge ID is the bridge priority (4 bits), the extended system ID that holds the VLAN (12 bits) and the switch MAC address. Cost and port ID are about ports, not the bridge.

6.cue: Match the STP protocol with the correct description

keys.k: multiple VLANs to run in a single

6.tip: STP = old, one tree for all. MSTP = Many VLANs share one tree. Rapid PVST+ = Rapid, Per VLAN, Cisco.
6.why: Original STP runs one tree for every VLAN. MSTP maps groups of VLANs to shared instances. Rapid PVST+ is Cisco's version of RSTP that runs one fast tree per VLAN.

7.cue: learn MAC addresses and process BPDUs
7.tip: You LEARN MACs in LEARNING and keep learning in FORWARDING. Blocking and listening don't learn.
7.why: In the learning state the port starts filling the MAC table but doesn't send data yet. In forwarding it sends data and keeps learning. Both still process BPDUs.

8.tip: STP always likes LOW: lowest priority, then lowest MAC. No IP addresses in STP.
8.why: If all switches keep the default priority, the tie is broken by the MAC address and the lowest one wins. STP is Layer 2, so IP addresses never matter.

9.cue: Match the spanning-tree feature with the protocol type

keys.k: reduces the number of STP instances

9.tip: PVST+ = Cisco's 802.1D. RSTP = Rapid 802.1D (802.1w). MSTP = fewer instances.
9.why: PVST+ is Cisco's per-VLAN take on classic 802.1D. RSTP (802.1w) is the faster version of 802.1D. MSTP is the IEEE standard that groups VLANs to cut down the number of trees.

10.cue: three ports are shown in the forwarding state
10.tip: Forwarding roles: Root and Designated (R and D). Alternate waits, disabled is off.
10.why: Root ports and designated ports carry traffic, so they sit in forwarding. Alternate ports are blocked as backups, and disabled ports are shut down.

11.cue: function of STP in a scalable network
11.tip: STP = Stop The Pathloops: it blocks extra paths so frames can't loop.
11.why: Redundant switch links can make frames loop forever. STP blocks the extra paths and keeps them as backups. Bundling links for bandwidth is EtherChannel, not STP.

12.tip: STP is ON out of the box on Cisco switches. CDP finds neighbors, not STP.
12.why: Cisco switches run spanning tree by default so loops are blocked as soon as you cable them. Layer 2 frames have no TTL, which is why STP is needed.

13.cue: only one root bridge so that traffic from all VLANs
13.tip: 802.1D = the original: one tree, one root, all VLANs. Anything with PV (per VLAN) has many.
13.why: Classic IEEE 802.1D builds one spanning tree for the whole network, so all VLANs use the same root and path. PVST+ and Rapid PVST build one tree per VLAN.

14.cue: purpose of the Spanning Tree Protocol
14.tip: STP = switches (Layer 2) loops. Routing loops are a router problem, not STP's job.
14.why: STP stops frames from circling forever between switches with redundant links. It does not split collision or broadcast domains and has nothing to do with routing.

15.cue: which port on a non-root bridge will become a root port
15.tip: Root port = cheapest road. Look at the PATH COST first.
15.why: A non-root switch adds up the cost of the links to the root bridge on each port and picks the lowest. Only on a tie does it look at sender bridge ID and port ID.

16.cue: Which switch will be the root bridge
16.tip: Same priority? Lowest MAC wins. Compare the last digits: 1111 is the smallest.
16.why: All four switches have priority 32769, so the lowest MAC address breaks the tie. S2 has 000A00031111, the lowest one, so it becomes the root bridge.

17.cue: turning spanning tree off and having multiple paths
17.tip: No STP = loops: broadcasts never die and the MAC table keeps flipping.
17.why: Without STP, a frame loops between switches forever, causing a broadcast storm. The same MAC keeps showing up on different ports, so the MAC table keeps changing.

18.cue: ensure that it becomes the root bridge
18.tip: Lower than default 32768, in steps of 4096: 32768 - 4096 = 28672.
18.why: Lower priority wins and the default is 32768. Priority must be a multiple of 4096, so 28672 beats every default switch. A value like 1 isn't valid.

19.cue: EtherChannel between S1 and the other two switches

keys.k: two different switches through the same EtherChannel

19.tip: EtherChannel = one bundle, two ends. Both ends must be the same two switches.
19.why: An EtherChannel bundles parallel links between the same two devices. You can't make one bundle that splits to two separate switches.

20.tip: PAgP = Port Aggregation protocol (Cisco only). LACP = the open standard.
20.why: PAgP was made by Cisco and only works on Cisco gear. LACP is the IEEE open standard. PAgP doesn't need an even number of ports.

21.cue: requirements to be able to configure an EtherChannel
21.tip: Bundle twins: same speed, same duplex, same VLAN settings.
21.why: All links in a bundle must act alike, so they need the same speed and duplex. The ports don't have to be next to each other on the switch.

22.cue: what can be determined about the EtherChannel bundle
22.tip: Protocol column says PAgP? That's Cisco's own. LACP would be the open one.
22.why: The output shows PAgP in the Protocol column, and PAgP is Cisco proprietary. The bundle is SU (Layer 2, in use) and uses Fa ports, not Gigabit.

23.cue: parameters must match on the ports of two switches to create a PAgP
23.tip: Match the link settings (speed, VLANs), not the identities (port ID, MAC).
23.why: Ports in a bundle must carry the same traffic the same way, so speed and VLAN settings must match. Port IDs and MACs are always different, and PAgP modes can differ (auto with desirable).

24.cue: effect after the commands are issued on SW1 and SW2
24.tip: ON talks to nobody. ON only pairs with ON.
24.why: SW1 is set to on, which sends no negotiation, while SW2 is desirable and waits for PAgP replies. On doesn't answer, so the bundle never forms.

25.cue: What change in configuration would correct the problem
25.tip: Auto needs a Desirable partner (PAgP). Active is LACP and can't talk to auto.
25.why: SW1 uses auto, a PAgP mode, but SW2 uses active, an LACP mode, so they speak different protocols. Making SW2 desirable lets it start PAgP and SW1 answers.

26.cue: one of the three interfaces is down
26.tip: Bundle loses a link? It just shrinks. The rest keep sharing the load.
26.why: EtherChannel is built for redundancy: if one link fails, traffic moves to the links still up and they keep load balancing. The channel doesn't fail.

27.tip: Auto + Desirable = PAgP pair. Passive + Active = LACP pair.
27.why: Auto only answers, it never starts negotiation. The other side must be desirable so it sends PAgP packets. Passive and active are LACP modes.

28.cue: open protocol standard ... bundle physical ports
28.tip: LACP = Link Aggregation Control Protocol: the open (IEEE 802.3ad) one. PAgP is Cisco only.
28.why: LACP is the IEEE standard for building EtherChannels, so any vendor can use it. PAgP does the same job but only on Cisco devices.

keys.k: allowed range of VLANs must be the same

29.tip: Trunk bundle? Both ends must allow the same VLAN list.
29.why: Every link in a trunk bundle must carry the same VLANs, so the allowed VLAN list must match on both switches. The ports don't need to be next to each other.

30.tip: LACP: Lets switches negotiate, works Across vendors.
30.why: LACP lets two connected switches agree on a bundle automatically, and as an open standard it works between different brands. It can't mix Fast and Gigabit ports.

31.cue: non-root port that is permitted to forward traffic
31.tip: Designated = the forwarding port on each segment that isn't a root port.
31.why: Root ports face toward the root. On each link, the port that forwards traffic onto it is the designated port. Alternate ports are blocked.

32.tip: EtherChannel = One link to STP, One place to configure.
32.why: STP sees the bundle as one link, so it doesn't block the extra cables. You configure the port-channel interface once and all member links get the same settings.

33.cue: port roles for ports A, B, C, and D
33.tip: Facing the root = root port. Root bridge ports = designated. The leftover blocked one = alternate.
33.why: C on S2 and D on S3 lead straight to the root S1, so they are root ports. B is on the root bridge, so it is designated. A on S2 toward S3 is the backup, so it is alternate.

34.tip: Aggregate links = EtherChannel. HSRP is gateway backup, PortFast is for end devices.
34.why: EtherChannel bundles several physical links into one logical link, adding up their bandwidth. Trunking just carries several VLANs and doesn't add links together.

35.cue: Port Aggregation Protocol ... S1 is configured to be in auto mode
35.tip: Auto waits, Desirable asks. Two waiters never meet.
35.why: Auto only replies to PAgP requests. If both sides were auto, nobody would start. S2 must be desirable so it sends the request.

36.cue: least likely for the switch to be selected as the root
36.tip: Highest valid priority = least likely root. Max is 61440 (15 x 4096). 65535 isn't valid.
36.why: Lower priority wins the root election, so the highest priority is the least likely. Priority comes in steps of 4096 up to 61440, so 65535 can't be set.

37.cue: PVST+ port states are MAC addresses learned
37.tip: LEARNING learns. FORWARDING keeps learning. Listening only listens to BPDUs.
37.why: MAC addresses are added to the table in the learning state and keep being learned in forwarding. Blocking and listening only handle BPDUs.

38.cue: lowest cost to reach the root bridge
38.tip: Cheapest way to the root = ROOT port.
38.why: Each non-root switch picks the port with the lowest cost to the root bridge as its root port, its main road toward the root.

39.cue: switch port closest, in terms of overall cost
39.tip: Closest to root = root port. Designated faces away from the root.
39.why: The port with the lowest total path cost to the root bridge is the root port. Designated ports forward away from the root onto each segment.

40.cue: field used to specify a VLAN ID
40.tip: Extended system ID = the VLAN tag inside the bridge ID.
40.why: The extended system ID is the 12-bit part of the bridge ID that holds the VLAN number, so each VLAN can have its own spanning tree.

41.cue: reference point for all path calculations
41.tip: Root bridge = the center of the tree. Every cost is measured to it.
41.why: STP measures every path cost from the root bridge. Each switch picks its root port by finding its cheapest way back to that one switch.

42.tip: 32768 = the default bridge PRIORITY. It's checked first, MAC only breaks ties.
42.why: Bridge priority is the first thing compared in the root election and starts at 32768. If priorities tie, the lowest MAC address decides.

43.tip: Trunks can bundle. EtherChannel works at Layer 2 or 3, max 8 active links.
43.why: EtherChannel bundles can be access or trunk links, so a trunk port can join one. It works at Layer 2 and Layer 3, supports up to 8 active links and can use PAgP.

44.cue: show etherchannel summary command on the switch S1
44.tip: SD = Something Down. I on the ports = stand-alone, not bundled.
44.why: Po1 shows SD, meaning the port channel is down, and each port shows I (stand-alone), so none joined the bundle. The EtherChannel isn't working.

45.tip: Many cables, one logical link. Up to 8, same speed only.
45.why: EtherChannel combines parallel physical links between two switches into one logical link. It allows up to 8 links and they must all be the same speed.

46.tip: PAgP modes: Desirable and Auto (D-A). LACP modes: Active and Passive (A-P). On = no protocol.
46.why: PAgP negotiates using desirable (starts the talk) and auto (waits and replies). Active and passive belong to LACP, and on uses no protocol at all.

47.tip: ON + ON = forced bundle, no talking. Every other mode negotiates.
47.why: Mode on forces ports into the channel without PAgP or LACP packets, so both ends must be on. Desirable, auto, active and passive all send negotiation traffic.

48.cue: interfaces do not form an EtherChannel
48.tip: Compare the allowed lines: 1-5,10 vs 1,5,10. Different lists = no bundle.
48.why: S1 allows VLANs 1-5,10 but S2 allows only 1,5,10. Trunk ports in an EtherChannel must carry the same VLANs on both ends, so the bundle won't form.

49.tip: ON = just turn it on, no talking. All other modes negotiate.
49.why: Mode on forces the interface into the bundle without PAgP or LACP. Active and desirable send negotiation packets, and auto waits for them.

50.tip: Balance by pairs: MAC to MAC or IP to IP. Keep it simple, no mixed combos.
50.why: EtherChannel picks which link to use by hashing address pairs, such as source and destination MAC or source and destination IP. That spreads flows across the links.

51.tip: MST = Multiple Spanning Tree: Many VLANs share a few trees (up to 16).
51.why: MST groups VLANs that share the same topology into a few RSTP instances instead of one per VLAN. It still supports PortFast, BPDU guard and the other add-ons.

52.cue: outcome of a Layer 2 broadcast storm
52.tip: Storm = switch is drowning. No room for new frames, so they get dropped.
52.why: In a broadcast storm, looping frames use up all the bandwidth and switch resources, so new traffic can't be handled and is dropped. Routers don't take over switching.

53.cue: design features require Spanning Tree Protocol
53.tip: Extra switches or extra links at Layer 2 = possible loops = need STP.
53.why: Redundant switch links and backup switches create more than one path, which can loop frames. STP blocks the extra paths. Routes and VLANs are other topics.

54.cue: one of the trunk links changes to a down state
54.tip: Lose one cable from a bundle of four? Still up with three.
54.why: EtherChannel keeps working as long as at least one member link is up. Traffic just moves to the remaining links, and STP doesn't notice since it sees one logical link.
